land.text: Saint-Domingue, the French colony in the west of Hispaniola, of which the slave rebels held the Northern Province ('By 1792, slave rebels controlled a third of Saint-Domingue')

predecessors.note: The saint-domingue dossier (am-06-x) ends the colony in August 1791 and hands the same land to this state in 1792. Sovereignty over the colony passed from France to Haiti only on 1 January 1804 (Dessalines' declaration at Gonaïves); between 1792 and 1803 the dossier follows the revolutionary polity that Cliopatria draws as 'Haiti' (see notes). Also French Directory 1796-1799 and French Consulate 1800-1804 as the colony's sovereign.

land.text: the same Haitian state under Cliopatria's third row, 'Republic of Haiti' 1936-2024

successors.note: Not a political end: this dossier stops where Cliopatria's 'Empire of Haiti' row stops (1915) plus the 1916-1935 years Cliopatria leaves empty; the Haitian state continues without a break under the 'republic-of-haiti' dossier.

capitals.name: Port-au-Prince
capitals.note: First Empire page infobox: capital Port-au-Prince; Dessalines was crowned at Cap-Haïtien in October 1804. The pages opened give no seat for 1792-1803, so none is drawn for those years. In the divided years 1806-1820 Port-au-Prince is the southern Republic's capital ('centered on Port-au-Prince', Haiti page); the northern State/Kingdom sat at Cap-Haïtien.

correction.text: the Northern Province, held by the slave rebels since August 1791; 'By 1792, slave rebels controlled a third of Saint-Domingue' (applies to 1792-1793; 1794-1799 is haiti_1794)

keyframe_review.note: 31,347 km2 is the whole western third of Hispaniola; the page says 'By 1792, slave rebels controlled a third of Saint-Domingue' and that in late August 1791 'slaves had taken control of the entire Northern Province', so for 1792-1793 only the north is the rebels'. Modern Haiti is 27,700 km2 in the Haiti infobox (27,750 in its Geography section; ratio 1.13, within range). From 1794 the whole-colony outline is kept as haiti_1794.

correction.text: the whole colony of Saint-Domingue as Cliopatria draws it and as the French side held it from May 1794 (see the gain of 1794); British-held Jérémie, Môle St Nicolas and Port-au-Prince are contest zones, and Rigaud's south is a contest zone in 1799 until March 1800

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1794-1799, the colony as the French side held it: the 6 May 1794 gain (ledger) explains the step from the north-only outline of 1792-1793 ('Louverture ... brought his forces over to the French side on 6 May 1794'; the French forces were 'Sonthonax commanding in the north and André Rigaud leading in the south'). Who held what is only partly on the pages: the British held Jérémie and Môle St Nicolas from September 1793 and Port-au-Prince from May 1794 to 18 May 1798 (contest events); the Saint-Domingue page has Louverture 'sole ruler of northern Saint-Domingue' after 1795, the Toussaint Louverture page makes him commander of the West Province in 1796 and, in 1798, 'in sole command of French Saint-Domingue, except for a semi-autonomous state in the south' under Rigaud, which the War of the South (June 1799 - 11 March 1800, contest events) ended. The page on the British occupation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_occupation_of_Saint-Domingue) could not be loaded; the Spanish zone of 1793-1795 and the Artibonite and Centre are not mapped on any page opened. Outside the north Louverture's rule is thus wider in this outline than in his own command before 1796-1798, which is why the confidence of the 1794 gain is 2.

31,347 km2 for the colony in 1800 and 1802: after Toussaint 'took Jacmel on 11 March 1800' the page says 'he ruled Saint Domingue as its dictator'. 1801 adds the east (haiti_1801); in 1802 the French landing of 2 February opens a contest over the whole outline (ledger).

correction.text: Saint-Domingue plus the former Spanish colony of Santo Domingo, invaded in December 1800

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1801: Louverture 'led an invasion of neighboring Santo Domingo (December 1800), and freed the slaves there on 3 January 1801', so the whole island is under his government for this year; Cliopatria draws only the west. The page does not date the loss of the east; it is put in 1802 (Saint-Domingue expedition page: Kerverseau took 'a large part of the Spanish area' in the February 1802 landings; confidence 2).

correction.text: the former colony whose independence Dessalines declared on 1 January 1804

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1803-1804, years Cliopatria leaves empty: the same colony outline, in rebel hands only as the French lose it ('the French abandoned Port-au-Prince on 8 October 1803', the Battle of Vertières on 18 November 1803, the last French soldiers boarded British ships on 30 November 1803) and independent from 1 January 1804. The contest over it ends in November 1803.

correction.text: unchanged for 1805-1806; 1807-1808 are described by haiti_1807 (the north under Christophe is no longer part of the state)

keyframe_review.note: 31,292 km2 stands for the Empire (22 September 1804 to Dessalines' death on 17 October 1806), 'located on the western portion of the island of Hispaniola'. From the end of 1806 the north is a separate state, so 1807-1808 are replaced by haiti_1807. The infobox gives no area.

minus.text: the north under Christophe: the three northern départements and the Artibonite (the pages draw no line)

correction.text: the southern Republic of Haiti under Pétion, centred on Port-au-Prince, without the northern State/Kingdom under Christophe

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1807-1819: after 17 October 1806 'Haiti became split into two' (Haiti page): the senate elected Pétion president of the southern Republic of Haiti, 'centered on Port-au-Prince', and Christophe led the northern State of Haiti, later the Kingdom (28 March 1811, Haiti infobox). Cliopatria draws the unified west for 1806-1821. None of the pages opened draws the line between the two. The north is read as the Nord, Nord-Est, Nord-Ouest and Artibonite départements (my reading; fix round: the Artibonite (department) page has Saint-Marc rebel 'against the crown' in 1820, Christophe's palace at Petite-Rivière-de-l'Artibonite and the department dissociating itself from Port-au-Prince 'notably under the leadership of Henry Christophe'; the State of Haiti, Kingdom of Haiti and Henri Christophe pages are silent on the frontier), and the south is the rest (Ouest, Centre, Sud-Est, Sud, Nippes, Grand'Anse).

correction.text: unchanged for 1820-1821; 1809-1819 are described by haiti_1807

keyframe_review.note: 31,347 km2 is the unified west and holds only for 1820-1821: the Unification page says the internal conflicts 'lasted until 1820 when Haitian president Jean-Pierre Boyer finally unified both the South and North of Haiti' (the Haiti page also says 'reunifying in 1820' but, in another sentence, 'Beginning in 1821'). 1809-1819 is haiti_1807. The east stays Spanish until the Republic of Spanish Haiti (1 December 1821).

correction.text: unchanged for 1822-1843; 1844-1845 are described by haiti_1844

keyframe_review.note: 83,656 km2 for the whole island is right for 1822-1843: 'On February 9, 1822, Boyer formally entered the capital city, Santo Domingo' and the island was 'united from Cape Tiburon to Cape Samana in possession of one government'. It ends in 1843, not 1845: 'On February 27, 1844, the Trinitarios declared independence from Haiti', 'effectively ending Haitian rule of eastern Hispaniola'; 1844-1845 are haiti_1844. The page gives no area (Cliopatria's west alone is 31,292 km2 against 27,700 km2 for modern Haiti in the Haiti infobox (27,750 in the Geography section), ratio 1.13).

correction.text: the western third of Hispaniola; the east is the Dominican Republic from 27 February 1844

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1844-1845: the west only, since Haitian rule in the east ended on 27 February 1844 and the Haitian armies of March 1844 and August 1845 were repelled (Dominican War of Independence page). Cliopatria still draws the whole island to 1845 and starts the Dominican Republic in 1846.

31,292 km2, the west. The frontier is soft: the war ran to 24 January 1856 and the Dominican War of Independence page says 'The frontier was not finalized until 1936'. Area against the Haiti page's 27,700 km2 (infobox): ratio 1.13.
31,347 km2, the west (the second empire 1849-1859 and the restored republic leave the outline unchanged). Ratio 1.13 against the Haiti page's 27,700 km2 (infobox).
31,292 km2 for 1865-1914, the same outline; unverified beyond the Haiti page and the frontier note (settled only in 1936).
31,292 km2 for 1915, the year the US Marines landed (28 July); the state stays on the map under occupation, so 1916-1935 continue it as haiti_1916.

correction.text: Haiti under US occupation, 1915-1934, still a state with its own territory

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1916-1935, years Cliopatria leaves empty between its 'Empire of Haiti' row (to 1915) and its 'Republic of Haiti' row (from 1936): the same outline, under US occupation from 28 July 1915 to 1 August 1934 (the last Marines left on 15 August 1934). The Haiti-Dominican frontier was settled in 1936 (Dominican War of Independence page: the Dominican Republic 'relinquished claims to Hinche, Las Caobas, San Miguel de la Atalaya, and San Rafael de la Angostura').

region.text: the entire Northern Province

ledger.note: 1792: the slave rebels of Saint-Domingue hold the Northern Province. 'By 1792, slave rebels controlled a third of Saint-Domingue'; in the days after the rising of August 1791 'slaves had taken control of the entire Northern Province'. Haiti proper is born on 1 January 1804 (below); this is the revolutionary polity Cliopatria draws as 'Haiti'.

region.text: Jérémie and the Môle St Nicolas peninsula

ledger.note: 1793: the British land in the west. 'On 20 September 1793, about 600 British soldiers from Jamaica landed at Jérémie' and Môle St. Nicolas, the main French naval base, 'surrendered to the Royal Navy peacefully' on 22 September.

region.text: Port-au-Prince and its plain

ledger.note: 1794: the British take Port-au-Prince. 'Troops under John Whyte arrived on 19 May 1794 and took Port-au-Prince'; the page gives no exact date for the capture, so the year is the page's and no month is recorded.

minus.text: the north the rebels already held, and the zones the British held (Jérémie, Môle St Nicolas, Port-au-Prince)

region.text: the rest of the colony, the west and south that the French side held ('Sonthonax commanding in the north and André Rigaud leading in the south'), without the British-held zones

ledger.note: 6 May 1794: Louverture joins the French and the revolutionary polity comes to stand for the whole colony. 'In May 1794, Toussaint suddenly joined the French and turned against the Spanish', he 'brought his forces over to the French side on 6 May 1794', and the French forces were then 'Sonthonax commanding in the north and André Rigaud leading in the south'; from here the dossier follows the colony as the French side held it, as Cliopatria's 'Haiti' shape does. The region is my reading (the page gives no map). Louverture's own rule was narrower at first: the Saint-Domingue page has him 'sole ruler of northern Saint-Domingue' after 1795, the Toussaint Louverture page makes him commander of the West Province in 1796 and in 1798 'in sole command of French Saint-Domingue, except for a semi-autonomous state in the south' under Rigaud.

region.text: Môle St Nicolas and Jérémie, the last British holdings

ledger.note: 1798: Maitland leaves the north-west. In late 1798 he withdrew from Môle St Nicolas 'as Toussaint took command of the fortress'. The page also says the British were then 'reduced to only holding the western peninsular towns of Mole St Nicholas in the north and Jeremie in the south'; Jérémie's fate is not on the page. Fix round: 'Rigaud took control of Jeremie without any cost to his forces, as Maitland withdrew his southern forces to Jamaica' (same page, 1798). The Armistice of March 30, 1798 page has the British leaving 'their last stronghold in the north of the country, Môle-Saint-Nicolas, on August 31, 1798', while the Haitian Revolution page has Maitland withdrawing the last of his forces from Môle 'in the end of 1798' (31 August is the agreement's date there); the year is kept and no month is recorded.

region.text: Port-au-Prince

ledger.note: 1798: 'On 18 May the British left Port-au-Prince.'

region.text: Rigaud's southern territory (the Sud, Grand'Anse, Nippes and Sud-Est départements, my reading of 'the South'); Jacmel was 'held by Mulatto forces under the command of Rigaud'

ledger.note: June 1799: the War of the South begins. 'In June 1799, Rigaud initiated the War of the South against Toussaint's rule' (the André Rigaud page: 'when Toussaint's army invaded Rigaud's territory'). The south had been Rigaud's command for the French side since 1794 and was, from 1798, 'a semi-autonomous state in the south' (Toussaint Louverture page); it stays inside this state's outline and is drawn contested until Rigaud falls.

region.text: Rigaud's southern territory (the Sud, Grand'Anse, Nippes and Sud-Est départements, my reading of 'the South'); Jacmel was 'held by Mulatto forces under the command of Rigaud'

ledger.note: 11 March 1800: Toussaint takes Jacmel and Rigaud flees, so the whole colony is Louverture's. 'On 11 March 1800, Toussaint took Jacmel and Rigaud fled on the French schooner La Diana'; 'Having made himself master of the island...' (same page), and 'After defeating Rigaud, Louverture became master of the whole French colony of Saint-Domingue' (Saint-Domingue page). The Toussaint Louverture page has Rigaud fleeing to Guadeloupe and France in August 1800 and the Rigaud page says only 'In 1800'; the dossier keeps the Haitian Revolution page's 11 March.

1801: Louverture's constitution. 'In 1801, Louverture issued a constitution for Saint-Domingue that decreed he would be governor-for-life'; he 'began to rule the country as an effectively autonomous entity' (the page gives no month).

region.text: the former Spanish colony of Santo Domingo

ledger.note: 1801: Louverture takes Santo Domingo. He 'led an invasion of neighboring Santo Domingo (December 1800), and freed the slaves there on 3 January 1801'. The First Empire page calls the colony 'under French control (1795-1809)'; Cliopatria draws it in its Spanish Empire shape, hence the counterpart.

region.text: a large part of the Spanish area, taken by Kerverseau's landing; the page does not say how much of the east

ledger.note: 1802: the French take the east from Louverture's brother. 'Landing at Santo Domingo with 2,000 men, General Kerverseau took possession of a large part of the Spanish area of the island', then 'headed by Toussaint's brother Paul Louverture' (Saint-Domingue expedition page). The sentence closes the paragraph of the February 1802 landings (Cap-Français 3 February, attack 5 February, Rochambeau 6 February) and carries no date of its own, so the year is the page's and no month is recorded; the page does not say how or when Paul Louverture's hold ended, nor whether Kerverseau took all of the east. The First Empire page has Santo Domingo 'under French control' when Dessalines besieged it in 1805 (Haitian Revolution page: expedition instructions 'to restore slavery, at least in the formerly Spanish-held part of the island').

region.text: the whole colony fought over by Leclerc's army and the rebels

ledger.note: 1802: the French expedition lands. 'The French arrived on 2 February 1802 at Le Cap'; Napoleon 'in 1802 sent an expedition of 20,000 soldiers' (Haiti page). Toussaint agreed to surrender on 6 May 1802 and was seized; Dessalines and Pétion 'switched sides again, in October 1802, and fought against the French'.

region.text: the whole colony

ledger.note: 1803: the last French fall. 'The French abandoned Port-au-Prince on 8 October 1803'; 'The last battle on land of the Haitian Revolution, the Battle of Vertières, occurred on 18 November 1803'; 'On the night of 30 November 1803, 8,000 French soldiers and hundreds of white civilians boarded the British ships.'

region.text: the former colony of Saint-Domingue

ledger.note: 1 January 1804: Dessalines declares Haiti independent at Gonaïves. 'On 1 January 1804, from the city of Gonaïves, Dessalines officially declared the former colony's independence' (Haiti page: 'proclaimed under the native name Haiti by Dessalines on 1 January 1804').

22 September 1804: Dessalines becomes emperor; the First Empire of Haiti. He was proclaimed 'Emperor for Life' as Jacques I; the page gives the coronation as 6 October (lead) and 8 October (body), at Cap-Haïtien. Infobox: 'Territory of the Empire of Haiti (1804-1806), located on the western portion of the island of Hispaniola.'

region.text: Santiago and Santo Domingo, the Spanish colony under French control

ledger.note: February 1805: Dessalines marches on the east. '25 February 1805: Dessalines captured Santiago with 30,000 men'; on 6 March the siege of Santo Domingo began (Santo Domingo is 'under French control' on the page).

region.text: Santo Domingo

ledger.note: March 1805: the siege is lifted. About three days after it began 'French frigates and brigantines arrived, and Dessalines abandoned the siege and withdrew to Haiti'; the east stays outside the empire.

17 October 1806: Dessalines is assassinated; Pétion becomes president of the southern Republic of Haiti. 'The senate elected Pétion president of the southern Republic of Haiti' (Haiti infobox: 'Southern Republic: 17 October 1806'). The dossier follows the southern republic, which Boyer later extends to the whole island.

region.text: the north under Christophe: the three northern départements and the Artibonite (Saint-Marc, Gonaïves); no page draws the line

ledger.note: October 1806: the north breaks away. 'Christophe led the northern State of Haiti', later 'Kingdom of Haiti' (28 March 1811, Haiti infobox), with Cap-Haïtien as its seat. The pages draw no boundary; the north is read as the Nord, Nord-Est, Nord-Ouest and Artibonite départements. Fix round: the Artibonite (department) page has Saint-Marc rebel 'against the crown' in 1820, Christophe's palace at Petite-Rivière-de-l'Artibonite, and the department dissociating itself from Port-au-Prince and the West 'notably under the leadership of Henry Christophe'; the State of Haiti, Kingdom of Haiti and Henri Christophe pages draw no line ('the frontier between the two states remained largely stable throughout Christophe's reign'). Centre and Ouest stay with Pétion's republic.

region.text: the north under Christophe: the three northern départements and the Artibonite (Saint-Marc, Gonaïves); no page draws the line

ledger.note: 1820: Boyer reunites the north and south. The internal conflicts 'lasted until 1820 when Haitian president Jean-Pierre Boyer finally unified both the South and North of Haiti' (the Haiti page also says 'Beginning in 1821'). Fix round: the reunited north includes the Artibonite, where Saint-Marc's revolt against the crown (Artibonite (department) page) preceded Christophe's death in October 1820.

region.text: the eastern two thirds of Hispaniola, the former Spanish colony of Santo Domingo

ledger.note: 9 February 1822: Boyer enters Santo Domingo and unites the island. 'On February 9, 1822, Boyer formally entered the capital city, Santo Domingo after its ephemeral independence', with 12,000 soldiers; the island was 'united from Cape Tiburon to Cape Samana in possession of one government'. The Republic of Spanish Haiti (proclaimed 1 December 1821 by Núñez de Cáceres) is the state that fell.

region.text: eastern Hispaniola

ledger.note: 27 February 1844: the east declares independence. 'On February 27, 1844, the Trinitarios declared independence from Haiti'; the Haitian forces surrendered, 'effectively ending Haitian rule of eastern Hispaniola' (Haiti page: 'Nationalist Dominican forces in eastern Hispaniola seized control of Santo Domingo on 27 February 1844').

region.text: the Haitian-Dominican frontier, fought over in 1844, 1845, 1849 and 1855-1856

ledger.note: March 1844: Haiti tries to retake the east. 'On March 7, 1844, Haiti's President Hérard ordered a blockade of Dominican ports'; three columns totalling 30,000 men set out on 10 March and were repelled; Haitian invasions followed in 1845 (6 August), 1849 (9 March, Soulouque) and November 1855.

26 August 1849: Soulouque makes himself emperor, the Second Empire. 'a second empire was established under Faustin Soulouque before the return of the republic in 1859' (infobox 'Second Empire: 26 August 1849').

region.text: the Haitian-Dominican frontier

ledger.note: 24 January 1856: the last Haitian invasion fails. Of the Dominican War of Independence 'ended on January 24, 1856'; at Sabana Larga 'some 8,000 Dominicans defeated 22,000 Haitians' (body text 27 January). The same page says Haiti 'finally recognized its independence in 1867'.
15 January 1859: Soulouque abdicates; the republic returns. 'Soulouque abdicated his throne on 15 January 1859.'

region.text: the whole of Haiti

ledger.note: 28 July 1915: US Marines land at Port-au-Prince. The occupation 'began on July 28, 1915, when 330' Marines landed; in September 1915 the Senate ratified the Haitian-American Convention giving the US 'security and economic oversight of Haiti for a 10-year period', and US officials 'wielded veto power over all governmental decisions'. Recorded from the occupied state's side (roles reversed).

region.text: the whole of Haiti

ledger.note: 1 August 1934: the occupation ends. 'The occupation ended on August 1, 1934'; 'The last contingent of Marines departed on August 15, 1934.'

region.text: the same state, Haiti, under Cliopatria's later row

ledger.note: 1935: bookkeeping end, not a political event. The Haitian state continues unbroken (Haiti page: 'U.S. forces occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934', infobox 'officially the Republic of Haiti'); Cliopatria's third row, 'Republic of Haiti', begins in 1936 and the 'republic-of-haiti' dossier carries it on. The map should keep the colour continuous.

wars.name: Haitian Revolution

zones.text: Saint-Domingue, fought over by rebels, French republicans, British and Spanish forces

wars.outcome: Rebel victory: the French lose the colony in 1803 (Vertières 18 November, evacuation 30 November) and Dessalines declares independence on 1 January 1804.
wars.note: The page dates the rising to August 1791; the dossier's life begins in 1792 with Cliopatria. Louverture fought for Spain first and joined the French on 6 May 1794.

wars.name: War of the South

zones.text: Rigaud's southern territory (the Sud, Grand'Anse, Nippes and Sud-Est départements, my reading of 'the South'); Jacmel was 'held by Mulatto forces under the command of Rigaud'

wars.outcome: Toussaint's victory: he took Jacmel on 11 March 1800, Rigaud fled, and Toussaint 'ruled Saint Domingue as its dictator'.
wars.note: 'In June 1799, Rigaud initiated the War of the South against Toussaint's rule'; the Andre Rigaud page dates the invasion of Rigaud's territory to June 1799 and the Toussaint Louverture page says it 'lasted more than a year' (Rigaud left in August 1800 on that page).

wars.name: Dessalines' invasion of Santo Domingo (1805)
wars.outcome: Failed: Dessalines took Santiago on 25 February, besieged Santo Domingo from 6 March and withdrew when French ships arrived; the east stayed outside the empire.
wars.note: Named from the First Empire page; the page also reports an April 1805 campaign of destruction.

wars.name: Dominican War of Independence

zones.text: the frontier between the Haitian west and the Dominican east

wars.outcome: Dominican victory: separation of the Santo Domingo territory from Haiti; Haitian offensives of 1844, 1845, 1849 and 1855-1856 failed (Sabana Larga, January 1856).

wars.name: United States occupation of Haiti
wars.outcome: American victory over the Cacos (First Caco War ended with the capture of Fort Rivière on 17 November 1915; the Second, 1918-1920, with Batraville's death); the occupation ended 1 August 1934. No border changed.
wars.note: Haiti stayed a state with its territory; its occupation is drawn hatched (rule 4).

certainty.note: The rebel, French, British and Spanish zones of 1792-1803 and the line between Christophe's north and Pétion's south in 1806-1820 are approximate; the pages name no boundary. The coasts are the island's own. The south in 1798-1800 was Rigaud's semi-autonomous state (Toussaint Louverture page) and is drawn contested in 1799-1800.
The island entire, 'from Cape Tiburon to Cape Samana', bounded by the sea.
The Haitian-Dominican frontier is approximate until 1936 ('The frontier was not finalized until 1936'); the coasts are sharp.

notes:
ONE STATE OR THREE ROWS. Cliopatria's 'Haiti' (1792-1802), 'Empire of Haiti' (1805-1915) and 'Republic of Haiti' (1936-2024) are one continuous Haitian polity; the first two share Wikidata Q2006756 and the README lists all three as name variants. This dossier follows the brief for the first two (one dossier under the earlier slug, both Names in cliopatria_names) and ends in 1935; the 'republic-of-haiti' dossier (another part) carries 1936 onward. The 1935 'dissolve' is a row boundary and the successor is the same state: the colour agent should give 'haiti', 'empire-of-haiti' and 'republic-of-haiti' one colour (colours.json currently has three, and 'empire-of-haiti' has no dossier of its own).

1792-1803. Haiti did not exist as a sovereign state before 1 January 1804. Cliopatria's 1792-1802 shape is the whole colony of Saint-Domingue, which the pages show as French (Louverture 'brought his forces over to the French side on 6 May 1794' and from 1801 ruled under a constitution making him governor-for-life, 'an effectively autonomous entity') and, from 1793, partly British. I kept the revolutionary polity on the map (as Cliopatria does) and recorded the British, French and Spanish contests as ledger events; the first keyframe is cut to the rebel-held Northern Province for 1792-1793. Fix round (2026-10-19): the step from the north-only outline of 1792-1793 to the whole colony is now the 6 May 1794 gain, and Rigaud's south is a contest zone (June 1799 - 11 March 1800) inside that outline rather than a gain of 1800. The pages draw no control map for 1794-1799: Louverture was 'sole ruler of northern Saint-Domingue' after 1795, commanded the West Province from 1796, and in 1798 commanded all but 'a semi-autonomous state in the south'; the outline follows the French side as a whole. The page on the British occupation could not be loaded (url not found).
